tagline.text: Four quiet coral islands floating in the Camotes Sea

location.label: Location
location.text: Off Inopacan and Hindang, Leyte (Leyte's west coast)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500–3,500 per person (per day, varies by group size)

items.credit: Maximilian Felkel / CC BY-SA 3.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A collective name for four islands — Digyo, Apid, Mahaba, and Himokilan — scattered off Inopacan and Hindang on Leyte's west coast. Emerald shallows, white coral sand, and uncrowded island scenery can all be explored in a single day aboard one outrigger boat.

Cuatro Islas is Spanish for "four islands." They float in the Camotes Sea off western Leyte, comprising Digyo, Apid, and Mahaba, which belong to Inopacan, and Himokilan, which belongs to neighboring Hindang. The surrounding waters are designated a protected landscape and seascape to safeguard the coral reefs and fishing grounds, with villagers themselves handling tourism guiding and environmental management.

Each of the four islands has its own character. The smallest, Digyo, is a picture-perfect island of palm groves ringed by white sand and coral-pebble beaches, and it appears in most Cuatro Islas photos. Apid and Himokilan have fishing villages where you can glimpse residents' simple daily life, while Mahaba, true to its name (meaning "long"), stretches out with quiet beaches and shallow shoals. At low tide, the shallow waters around the islands turn a pale jade color, perfect for snorkeling and wading.

This isn't a place with big resorts and full amenities like Boracay or Cebu. The islands have almost no restaurants or shops, so you need to bring your own food and water, and getting there takes a bit of effort. In exchange, there are few tourists, so you can practically have an island to yourself for the day, and the sunset over the Camotes Sea in the late afternoon is spectacular.

It suits travelers passing through Leyte's west coast via Ormoc, Baybay, or Hilongos, and families or groups of friends who want to swim and snorkel around a quiet island. It's also an easy boat ride from Cebu, making it a good weekend island getaway for Cebu residents.
The most photogenic of the four islands. White coral sand and clear water spread beneath the shade of palm trees, and the island is small enough to walk around entirely.

The shallow coral reefs around the islands offer views of tropical fish and coral. Being a protected area, fish are relatively abundant, and your boatman will guide you to whichever spot suits the day's water conditions.

Charter an outrigger boat from the Inopacan coast to visit two or three islands or more in a day. Each island has its own mood, so moving between them is part of the fun, and the view of Leyte's mountains from the sea along the way is lovely too.

blocks.title: A Walk Through Apid Island's Fishing Village

children.text: On inhabited Apid Island, you can see the everyday life of a Leyte island community — fishing boats and mending nets, children playing on the beach. Ask permission before taking photos.
True to its name, this island stretches out long, with a beach you can walk far along. The shallow shoals exposed at low tide are good for wading.

blocks.title: Watching the Sunset Over the Camotes Sea

children.text: Since the islands sit west of Leyte, the sun sets directly over the water in the late afternoon. You can also enjoy the sunset beyond the four islands from the Inopacan or Hindang coast.

With almost no restaurants on the islands, the local way to enjoy them is a picnic — buy fish, meat, and fruit at the Inopacan market and grill it at a cottage. Ask your boatman in advance whether grilling is allowed.

Camping on the islands requires permission from the local government and island management, and the rules can change, so be sure to check with the Inopacan tourism office beforehand.

3 hours 30 minutes to 4 hours
by car via Baybay.

Flying into Mactan-Cebu Airport (CEB) and crossing by boat to Leyte's west coast is also common. Airfares are often cheaper with more flight options, so travelers coming from Korea may find this route more convenient.
Ferries to Hilongos run daily from Cebu port, taking about
3 hours 30 minutes to 4 hours
. From Hilongos to Inopacan is about
30–40 minutes

You can also take the Cebu–Ormoc fast ferry (about
2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours

) and head south from Ormoc. There's also a ferry from Ubay in Bohol to Hilongos, letting you link this trip with a Bohol itinerary. Schedules and fares change often, so check the shipping line's notices.

There's essentially no scheduled ferry to the islands — you charter an outrigger boat from the Inopacan coast. It takes about
20–45 minutes
to reach the islands, and the fare runs about
per boat, depending on the number of islands and passengers. Boats can run short on weekends and holidays, so book a day ahead.
Leyte's west coast gets less rain than the eastern Pacific side, and
February–June
, with calm seas and clear skies, is best for island hopping.

From
July to December
, typhoons and low-pressure systems bring frequent rain and rough seas, sometimes cancelling outrigger sailings. During
November–January
, the northeast monsoon can roughen the sea in the afternoon, so it's safer to set out early in the morning and return early. On weekends during Holy Week and summer break (

The Cuatro Islas themselves have almost no lodging, so most people stay at small beach resorts or guesthouses on the Inopacan or Hindang coast. Prices run about

a night, and choosing a beachfront room facing the four islands lets you enjoy the sunset from your room. Since options are limited, book ahead during peak season, or, if you need more choices, stay about
30 minutes
away in Hilongos or about
1 hour
away in Baybay.

With almost no restaurants or shops on the islands, it's typical to buy fish, squid, pork, rice, and fruit at the Inopacan market and bring it along. Grilling fish over charcoal at an island cottage and dipping it in a sauce of soy sauce, chili, and calamansi is the local way to enjoy an island picnic. Leyte's signature snacks binagol and moron, and Baybay's coconut sweets, are also worth trying along the way.
There are no shops on the islands, so bring plenty of drinking water, food, ice, and trash bags.

The per-person cost of an outrigger boat drops as group size grows. Before departing, clearly settle which islands are included, the waiting time, and whether the environmental fee is included in the fare.
Bringing your own snorkel gear and aqua shoes makes things easier — coral pebbles and sea urchins can hurt bare feet.
Shade is scarce, so bring a hat, a rash guard, and reef-safe sunscreen.
The sea is often calmest in the morning. It's best to set out early and return before the afternoon wind picks up.
ATMs are scarce in Inopacan and Hindang. Get cash in Ormoc, Baybay, or Hilongos beforehand.
Some islands have weak phone signal, so agree on a return time and meeting spot with your boatman in advance.

The waters around the islands are a protected area. Collecting coral and shells, catching marine life, and littering are prohibited, and violations can be fined. Environmental fees and visit rules can change under local government policy, so check the latest notices.
Wear a life vest when riding the outrigger boat, and postpone your trip if the waves are high or the sky looks threatening.
The channels between the islands can have fast currents in places, so don't swim far from the beach.
The midday sun is very strong, creating a risk of heatstroke and sunburn. Drink water often and rest in the shade.
There are no medical facilities on the islands, so bring basic first-aid supplies and vinegar in case of a jellyfish sting.
On inhabited islands, behave quietly, and ask permission before photographing private property or homes.
